effect_estimate.comment: Combines descriptive longitudinal proportions on tenure-based tapstand access and council attendance with inferential t-test and repeated-measures ANOVA results on seasonal water insecurity and social-network enforcement.
effect_estimate.value: Landowning community members (53%) and proxy members including anticrético holders (29%) were eligible for community tapstand water and Neighborhood Council voting, whereas renters (18%) were formally excluded (Table 1). Across 5 seasonal waves, legitimate community members accounted for 81.0%–87.5% of households accessing tapstand water while free-riding renters accounted for 12.5%–19.0% (baseline April–May 2004: 85% legitimate beneficiaries vs. 15% renters; Table 4). Household water insecurity (9-point Guttman scale) varied significantly across seasons (repeated-measures ANOVA F(3,54)=4.24, Wilks' lambda=0.81, p=0.009, eta squared=0.19; rising from mean 2.8 [SD 2.7] in Wet Season 2 to 3.9 [SD 2.5] in Dry Season; Table 3), prompting uniform dry-season rationing of tapstand allotments from 40 L to 20 L per household/day. Community members comprised 88.8%–100.0% of Neighborhood Council attendees when functioning normally, though renter attendance rose to 50.0% during a presidential corruption dispute (Table 5). Community members maintained significantly larger rule-enforcing social networks than renters (mean 11.1 [SD 9.6] vs. 6.0 [SD 4.1], t(55)=3.17, p=0.002; Table 6), with significant seasonal variation in network size (F(4,53)=4.09, Wilks' lambda=0.76, p=0.006, eta squared=0.24; Table 7) and no significant season-by-membership interaction (F(4,52)=0.09, Wilks' lambda=0.99, p=0.99, eta squared=0.01; Table 8).
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF p. 5–11, Tables 1–8 and Results text

mechanism_certainty.comment: Mixed-methods study (design ceiling = 2 under CODEBOOK.md §9) in which the researcher lived in Villa Israel and directly observed daily tapstand operations, punch-card verification, tenure-based renter exclusion, supervisor discretion, rule violations, and Neighborhood Council meetings, alongside 5-wave household panel measurements.
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF p. 4–10, Methods and How Villa Israel's Water Institution Functions

mechanism_flags.comment: Villa Israel lies outside SEMAPA's municipal water network (service_area) and restricts community tapstand eligibility and council voting to settlement landowners and proxy/anticrético occupants while excluding renters (tenure, property). Eligible users must attend monthly council meetings, contribute labor/materials to user groups, pay a 10-boliviano bimonthly fee, wait within a 4:00–9:00 am contiguous turn-taking window, and present a yellow punch card (participation, fees, procedural_steps, documentation). Monitoring and sanctioning occur across 4 levels including a paid tapstand supervisor who exercises discretion over rule disputes and seasonal rationing, while user groups informally accommodate verified subsistence need by ~15% free-riding renters (sanction, discretion, hardship_exception).

outcome_flags.comment: Directly measured household tapstand water access across 5 seasons (Table 4) and 9-item water insecurity (Table 3), daily household water allotments cut from 40 L to 20 L and per-capita task quantities (Table 2; 72% below 50 lpcd), scheduled intermittent opening in 20-minute blocks 6 days/week between 4:00 and 9:00 am, and frequent mid-sequence dry-outs causing unpredictable daily delivery timing.
outcome_flags.where_found: PDF p. 5–9, Tables 2–4 and Appendix (PDF p. 12–13)

risk_of_bias_tool.comment: Genuine mixed-methods study integrating primary qualitative fieldwork (participant observation across wet/dry seasons 2003–2004, 2 months of key informant interviews, open-ended ethnographic notes, and 2008 semi-structured follow-up visits) with a primary quantitative 5-wave randomly sampled household panel survey (N=72) analyzed via descriptive statistics, t-tests, and repeated-measures ANOVAs.

sample_size.comment: 96 households were randomly sampled from a community map of 415 residential constructions in Villa Israel and 72 households (75%) participated across 5 panel waves at 2-month intervals (1 primary knowledgeable respondent analyzed per household; complete-case analytic N=57–58 in repeated-measures ANOVAs/t-test in Tables 3 and 6–8).
sample_size.value: 72 randomly selected households in 1 urban squatter settlement (Villa Israel, out of 96 contacted from 415 residential constructions; 5 interview waves at 2-month intervals over 10 months), supplemented by participant observation, key informant interviews, and 2008 follow-up interviews

study_design.comment: Two-stage mixed-methods study combining ethnographic participant observation (2003–2004) and key-informant interviews with a 10-month, 5-wave longitudinal panel survey of 72 randomly selected households (2004–2005) and 2008 follow-up visits.
study_design.value: Mixed-methods ethnographic and longitudinal household panel study (participant observation, key informant interviews, and 5-wave repeated-measures household panel survey with t-test and repeated-measures ANOVA)
